title: Simple circuits: why a bulb lights only in a complete loop

summary.text: A torch bulb lights only when electricity can flow from a cell, through the bulb and all the way back to the cell. This complete loop is called a circuit. A gap anywhere in it, and the bulb goes out at once. Metals let electricity through, so they are called conductors. Plastic, rubber, wood, paper and glass do not, so they are called insulators. A wall socket in India is 230 volts and can kill, so we experiment only with small 1.5 volt cells. Inside the wire, tiny particles called electrons are pushed round the loop by the cell, and they come back to it.
summary.art: A child's hands holding an AA cell in a holder, two wires and a small glowing torch bulb, with a dotted arrow running round the loop from the cell, through the bulb and back to the cell.

intro.hook: Try this with a grown-up. Stand a torch bulb on top of an AA cell. It does not light. Now add one wire, in the right place, and it shines. Why does the bulb need that one extra wire?
intro.text: Electricity must go out of the cell, through the bulb, and come back to the cell. It needs a full loop. In this unit you build loops with cells, wires, foil and paper clips. You find out which things let electricity through and which stop it. You make your own switch. You learn why the sockets on the wall are never for experiments. And you find out what is really moving inside a wire.
intro.art: A torch bulb balanced on top of an AA cell, dark, and next to it the same bulb glowing, with a short wire joining the bulb's metal side to the bottom of the cell.

outcomes: I can name things at home that use electricity, and say which ones use mains electricity from the wall and which use cells.
I can say the safety rules for electricity and the reason for each one: never touch sockets, plugs or bare wires, never with wet hands, and only grown-ups plug things in.
I can build a complete circuit with a cell, wires and a bulb, and trace with my finger the path the electricity takes.
I can explain why a bulb goes out when the circuit is broken anywhere, and find the break in a circuit that does not work.
I can test materials with a circuit tester and sort them into conductors and insulators, and say that most conductors are metals.
I can make a switch from a paper clip and explain how it opens and closes a circuit.
I can tell how Galvani and Volta argued about frog legs, and how Volta's experiments led to the first battery.

terms.meaning: A kind of energy that flows along wires and makes things work, such as lights, fans and phones.
terms.example: When you switch on a ceiling fan, electricity flows through it and makes it turn.
terms.art: A ceiling fan turning, with a wire running from it to a switch on the wall.

terms.meaning: A small store of energy that pushes electricity round a circuit. People often call it a battery.
terms.example: An AA cell in a TV remote. It is 1.5 volts.
terms.art: An AA cell with its flat end marked minus and its bumpy end marked plus.

terms.meaning: Two or more cells joined together. In everyday talk, people also call a single cell a battery.
terms.example: A TV remote with two AA cells side by side is using a battery of two cells.
terms.art: The back of a TV remote opened, showing two AA cells lying head to tail.

terms.meaning: One of the two ends of a cell where wires are joined. One is marked plus (+) and the other minus (−).
terms.example: The small bump on top of an AA cell is its plus terminal. The flat bottom is its minus terminal.
terms.art: An AA cell with arrows pointing to the bump marked + and the flat end marked −.

terms.meaning: A complete loop that electricity can flow all the way round, from the cell and back to the cell.
terms.example: In a torch, electricity flows from the cells, through a metal strip, through the bulb and back to the cells.
terms.art: A loop of wire joining a cell and a bulb, with arrows going round.

terms.meaning: A circuit with no gaps. A bulb lights only in a complete circuit.
terms.example: When the wire touches both the cell and the bulb, the loop is complete and the bulb lights.
terms.art: A glowing bulb in a closed loop of wire, with a tick beside it.

terms.meaning: A circuit with a gap somewhere. Electricity cannot cross the gap, so nothing works. It is also called an open circuit.
terms.example: If a wire slips off the cell, the bulb goes dark.
terms.art: A dark bulb in a loop of wire with one end lifted away from the cell, and a cross beside it.

terms.meaning: A small glass lamp with a very thin wire inside, called a filament. The filament gets so hot that it glows.
terms.example: An old torch bulb has a tiny coiled filament you can see through the glass.
terms.art: A close-up of a torch bulb with its thin coiled filament glowing orange.

terms.meaning: A part that opens and closes a gap in a circuit, so you can turn things off and on.
terms.example: The light switch on your wall opens and closes a gap in the wire to the light.
terms.art: A paper clip switch on a piece of cardboard, shown open and then closed.

terms.meaning: A material that lets electricity flow through it easily. Most conductors are metals.
terms.example: Copper wire, a steel spoon and aluminium foil are all conductors.
terms.art: A steel spoon, a coin, a paper clip and a strip of foil in a row, each with a small glowing bulb above it.

terms.meaning: A material that does not let electricity flow through it. Plastic, rubber, wood, glass, paper and cloth are insulators.
terms.example: The plastic around a fan wire is an insulator. It keeps the electricity inside the copper.
terms.art: A cut wire showing shiny copper inside and a coloured plastic coat around it.

terms.meaning: The electricity that comes to wall sockets from power stations. In India it is 230 volts. It can kill.
terms.example: The fridge, the mixer and the iron are plugged into the mains.
terms.art: A plug in a wall socket, with a red warning sign beside it.

terms.meaning: The unit for how hard a cell or supply pushes electricity. The short form is V.
terms.example: An AA cell is 1.5 volts. A wall socket in India is 230 volts, about 150 times as much.
terms.art: A small AA cell labelled 1.5 V next to a wall socket labelled 230 V.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle found in every atom. It has an electric charge. In metals, some electrons can move about freely.
terms.example: When a bulb lights, electrons are moving through the wire and the filament.
terms.art: A zoomed-in drawing of a wire, showing tiny dots drifting along inside it.

terms.meaning: A path where electricity goes straight from one end of a cell to the other, with nothing like a bulb on the way. The wire gets hot and the cell runs down fast.
terms.example: Never join the two ends of a cell with just a wire or a strip of foil.
terms.art: A cell with a wire joining its two ends directly, a red cross over it.

terms.meaning: The harm done when electricity flows through a person's body. Mains electricity can burn and can stop the heart.
terms.example: Touching a bare wire that is plugged in can give an electric shock.
terms.art: A damaged wire with bare copper showing, and a hand stopping well away from it.

explanations.definition: Electricity is a kind of energy. Electrical appliances use it to make light, sound, heat, cold and movement.
explanations.description: Look around any home in India and you find electricity at work. Tube lights and LED bulbs make light. A TV and a doorbell make sound. An iron, a geyser and an induction stove make heat. A fridge makes things cold. A ceiling fan and a mixer-grinder make movement. Some appliances do two jobs. A TV makes light and sound. A fan makes movement, and the moving air cools you. When the power goes off, all of these stop at once. Only the things with their own cells or batteries keep working, such as a torch, a phone or a wall clock.
examples: A mixer-grinder turns electricity into movement, and its loud whirr is sound.
A phone runs on its own battery, so it keeps working in a power cut until the battery runs down.
An inverter keeps a few lights and fans on in a power cut, using big batteries charged earlier.
explanations.art: A home with labels on its appliances: a tube light for light, a TV for sound, an iron for heat, a fridge for cold and a fan for movement.
explanations.context: This card is about the many ways a home uses electricity, and what still works in a power cut.

explanations.definition: Mains electricity is made in power stations and comes to our homes along wires. In India it is 230 volts. A cell is a small, portable store of energy, usually 1.5 volts.
explanations.description: Power stations make electricity from burning coal, falling water, wind, sunlight or the heat of splitting atoms. Thick wires on tall towers carry it across the country to every town. Smaller wires bring it into your home, to the switches and sockets in the wall. This is mains electricity. It pushes very hard, at 230 volts. That is strong enough to push electricity through a person's body, and it can kill. A cell works differently. Chemicals inside it react and push electricity round a circuit. An AA cell pushes at only 1.5 volts. It is too weak to push enough electricity through your dry skin for you to notice anything. That is why all the experiments in this unit use AA cells, and never the wall socket.
examples: The Shivanasamudra power station on the Kaveri river in Karnataka began making electricity from falling water in 1902.
A wall clock uses one AA cell for many months.
A big solar panel on a roof makes electricity from sunlight.
explanations.art: On one side, a power station by a river with tall towers carrying wires towards a town. On the other side, a child's hand holding a single AA cell.
explanations.context: Where does the electricity in your home come from? And how is it different from the electricity in a cell? This card explains.

explanations.definition: Mains electricity can push electricity through your body and give you an electric shock, which can kill. Water and damaged wires make shocks more likely.
explanations.description: Your body is mostly water with salts dissolved in it, and salty water lets electricity through. Dry skin slows electricity down a lot. Wet skin slows it much less. That is why you must never touch a switch, a plug or an appliance with wet hands. The plastic on a wire is an insulator that keeps the electricity inside the copper. If the plastic is cracked or burnt, the bare copper can give a shock, so stay away and tell a grown-up. Never push anything into a socket. Never pull a plug out by its wire. Never fly a kite near overhead power lines. Only grown-ups plug in, unplug and move mains appliances. Cells need care too. Never open, bite or burn a cell. Keep small round button cells away from babies, because a swallowed button cell can badly burn the food pipe in as little as two hours.
examples: A grown-up switches off the socket before pulling out the plug.
In many homes, the geyser switch is outside the bathroom, away from water.
If a kite gets stuck on a power line, leave it there and tell a grown-up.
explanations.art: A child drying their hands on a towel before a grown-up switches on a light, and a kite caught on a power line with a red cross beside it.
explanations.context: This card gives the safety rules for electricity, and the reason behind each rule.

explanations.definition: A circuit is a complete loop that electricity can flow round, from one terminal of the cell, through the parts of the circuit, and back to the other terminal.
explanations.description: A cell has two terminals, plus and minus. Electricity flows only when there is a path from one terminal to the other. A bulb has two contacts too. One is the metal tip at its bottom. The other is the metal side around its screw. The thin filament inside joins them. So the loop goes like this. From the plus terminal, along a wire, into the bulb's tip, through the filament, out of the bulb's side, along a second wire, and back to the minus terminal. If you stand a bulb on top of a cell, only the tip touches. The bulb's side has no path back to the bottom of the cell, so it stays dark. Add one wire from the bulb's side to the bottom of the cell, and the loop is complete.
examples: In a torch, a spring and metal strips join the cells, the switch and the bulb into one loop.
A bulb holder has two screws. One joins to the bulb's tip and one to its side.
A bulb lights whichever way round the cell is joined. An LED lights only one way round.
explanations.art: A torch bulb on an AA cell, with a dotted path drawn from the cell's top through the bulb's tip, round the filament, out of its side, down a wire and into the cell's bottom.
explanations.context: Why does a bulb need two wires, or one wire and a cell touching it? This card shows the full loop the electricity takes.

explanations.concept: Why a broken circuit stops everything
explanations.definition: If there is a gap anywhere in a circuit, the electricity stops flowing everywhere in the circuit at once.
explanations.description: It does not matter where the gap is. Lift the wire off the cell, or off the bulb, or cut it in the middle, and the bulb goes dark at once. This is because electricity is not like water poured into a bucket. It does not fill the bulb and stay there. It flows round and round the loop, back to the cell, for as long as the loop is whole. When the loop is broken, the flow stops everywhere together, like a cycle chain that has come off. A loose connection is the most common reason a circuit will not work. Other reasons are a flat cell, a broken filament, or a part made of an insulator.
examples: A torch that flickers usually has a loose spring or a dirty contact.
When one bulb in an old string of festival lights breaks, the whole string can go dark.
A rusty or greasy spring in a torch can stop the loop, because rust is a poor conductor.
explanations.art: Three loops, each with a dark bulb and a gap in a different place: next to the cell, next to the bulb, and in the middle of a wire.
explanations.context: This card explains why a gap anywhere in a circuit stops the bulb, and how to find the gap.

explanations.definition: A conductor is a material that lets electricity flow through it easily. An insulator is a material that does not.
explanations.description: Metals are good conductors. Copper, aluminium, iron, steel and brass all conduct. That is why wires are made of copper. Plastic, rubber, wood, glass, paper, cloth and dry air are insulators. That is why wires are wrapped in plastic. The metal inside carries the electricity, and the plastic outside keeps it in, away from our hands. Some things are in between. The graphite in a pencil is not a metal, but it conducts a little, so a bulb may glow dimly through it. Tap water conducts a little, because of the salts dissolved in it. Salty water conducts better. Watch out for coatings. A paper clip covered in coloured plastic will not conduct until you scrape the plastic off one spot.
examples: A plug has metal pins, which carry electricity, inside a plastic cover, which you hold.
A screwdriver for electricians has a steel tip and a thick plastic handle.
Electricians' gloves are made of rubber.
explanations.art: A plug cut in half lengthwise, showing copper wires and brass pins inside, wrapped in plastic.
explanations.context: Why are wires made of copper with plastic around them? This card explains which materials let electricity through and which do not.

explanations.definition: A switch is a part of a circuit that can open a gap, to stop the electricity, and close it, to let the electricity flow.
explanations.description: When a switch is on, two pieces of metal inside it touch, and the circuit is complete. When it is off, the metal pieces move apart, and there is a gap of air. Air is an insulator, so the electricity stops. You can make your own switch with a steel paper clip and two drawing pins on a piece of cardboard. Push the pins in, about 2 centimetres apart, and join a wire to each. Hook the paper clip round one pin. Swing it onto the other pin, and the circuit is complete. Swing it away, and the circuit is broken. The cardboard must be an insulator, or the electricity would go through it. Switches come as press switches, like a doorbell, rocker switches, like a wall switch, and slide switches, like many torches.
examples: A wall switch is a rocker switch.
A doorbell button is a press switch. It is on only while you press it.
Many torches have a slide switch.
explanations.art: A paper clip switch on cardboard, shown twice: open, with a dark bulb, and closed, with a glowing bulb.
explanations.context: How does a switch turn a light on and off? This card shows what happens inside it, and how to make one.

explanations.concept: What is moving in the wire
explanations.definition: An electric current is a flow of electric charge. In a metal wire, the charge is carried by electrons, tiny particles that are in every atom.
explanations.description: Every atom has electrons. In a metal, some of the electrons are not held tightly by any one atom. They drift about inside the metal. So a copper wire is already full of electrons, all the way round the loop, before you join it to a cell. The cell pushes on all of them at once, and they all start moving round together. That is why the bulb lights the moment you close the loop, even if the wire is two metres long. Each electron moves very slowly, less than a millimetre each second. The cell does not fill the wire with electrons, and the bulb does not use them up. The same electrons go round and come back. What the cell uses up is the energy stored in its chemicals. When that runs out, the cell is flat. In plastic, the electrons are held tightly by their atoms, so they cannot flow. That is why plastic is an insulator.
examples: A cycle chain moves all at once when you push the pedal. Every link moves, though no link goes fast.
A tube full of marbles: push one in at one end, and one pops out at the other end at once.
The arrows on circuit drawings go from plus to minus. People drew them that way before electrons were found in 1897. The electrons actually move from minus to plus.
explanations.art: A zoomed-in circle on a copper wire, showing tiny dots spread all along it, all drifting the same way, next to a cycle chain going round its gears.
explanations.context: When a bulb lights, what is actually moving inside the wire? This card explains.

explanations.definition: Nerves, muscles and many plants send signals using tiny charged particles that move in and out of their cells.
explanations.description: In 1791, an Italian doctor called Luigi Galvani said that living bodies use electricity. He was right. Your brain sends signals along your nerves to your muscles. Each signal is carried by charged particles moving in and out of the nerve cells. This is how you move your fingers. Your heart beats because of electrical signals, which a doctor can record with an ECG machine. Plants use electrical signals too. A touch-me-not plant feels a touch, and an electrical signal travels along their leaf stalk, so the leaves fold. Jagadish Chandra Bose measured electrical signals in plants in Kolkata over a hundred years ago. Some fish, like the electric eel of South America, store up so much charge that they can give a shock of more than 600 volts.
examples: A doctor puts sticky pads on your chest to record your heart's electrical signals.
The leaves of a touch-me-not fold within a second or two of a touch.
An electric eel uses shocks to stun the fish they hunt.
explanations.art: A touch-me-not plant folding their leaves as a finger touches them, with a faint zig-zag line running along the stem, next to an ECG line on a screen.
explanations.context: Wires and cells are not the only places with electricity. This card is about the electricity inside living things.

agreed.text: A bulb or other part works only in a complete circuit, a loop from one terminal of the cell back to the other.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can test it with a cell, a wire and a bulb. Lift any connection and the bulb goes out.

agreed.text: Metals are good conductors. Plastic, rubber, wood, glass and paper are insulators.
agreed.evidence: Testing materials with a circuit tester, as in this unit, gives the same result every time. Scientists have measured how well thousands of materials conduct.

agreed.text: In a metal wire, the electric current is carried by electrons.
agreed.evidence: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897. Later experiments showed that electrons carry the current in metals.

agreed.text: Mains electricity can kill, and wet skin lets electricity through much more easily than dry skin.
agreed.evidence: Doctors and electrical engineers have studied electric shocks for over a hundred years. Safety rules all over the world are based on this.

agreed.text: A cell does not make electric charge. It uses the energy of a chemical reaction to push charge round a circuit.
agreed.evidence: Volta's pile, built in 1799, and every cell since then work this way. When the chemicals are used up, the cell stops pushing.

challenging.claim: A cell is full of electricity, and the bulb uses it up.
challenging.who: A very common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: A cell does run down, and a flat cell will not light a bulb, so it seems something has been used up.
challenging.against: The electrons that flow come back to the cell, and the same number go round all the time. What runs out is the energy stored in the cell's chemicals.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that a cell is like a tank of electricity that empties.

challenging.claim: Electricity only needs to get from the cell to the bulb. One wire should be enough.
challenging.who: Many children, when they first try to light a bulb
challenging.for: A water pipe needs only to go from the tank to the tap. It seems electricity should be the same.
challenging.against: Stand a bulb on a cell with one wire to its tip only, and it stays dark. It lights only when there is a path back to the other terminal of the cell.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that electricity travels one way, from the cell to the bulb, and stops there.

challenging.claim: All metal things conduct, so a coloured paper clip will light the bulb.
challenging.who: A natural guess in the conductor test
challenging.for: Paper clips are made of steel, and steel is a conductor.
challenging.against: A paper clip with a plastic coat does not light the bulb, because the plastic is an insulator. Scrape a little plastic off each end, and it conducts.
challenging.context: This card is about a surprise in the conductor test: a metal thing that does not conduct.

challenging.claim: A small cell cannot hurt anyone, so any cell is safe for children.
challenging.for: You cannot feel any shock from an AA cell, even when you touch both ends.
challenging.against: An AA cell is safe to touch, but a swallowed button cell can badly burn a child's food pipe in as little as two hours. A shorted cell can make a wire hot. Cells that are opened or burnt can leak harmful chemicals or burst.
challenging.context: This card is about why even small cells need care.

challenging.claim: The electricity in a frog's legs came from the frog's own body.
challenging.for: The legs twitched when touched with metal, and Galvani later made them twitch with no metal at all, using the frog's own nerve.
challenging.against: Alessandro Volta showed that two different metals with something wet between them make electricity, with no frog at all. Both were partly right. Volta's metals made the first battery, and Galvani's animal electricity is real too: nerves really do use electrical signals.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous argument between two scientists, where each was partly right.

big_questions.q: The electrons were already in the wire before you joined it to the cell. So what did the cell actually give the bulb?
big_questions.hint: Think about what runs out when a cell goes flat, and what goes round and comes back.

big_questions.q: Why does a copper wire let electricity through, while the plastic around it does not?
big_questions.hint: Think about whether the electrons in each material are free to move, or held tight by their atoms.

big_questions.q: Your nerves carry electrical signals. Is a thought a kind of electricity, or something more?
big_questions.hint: Scientists can measure the signals in a brain. Can they measure what it feels like to have a thought?

big_questions.q: Nerve cells do not quite touch. A signal must cross a tiny gap between one nerve cell and the next. Is that gap a kind of switch?
big_questions.hint: A switch decides when electricity can cross. Think about when a signal in your body crosses the gap, and when it stops.

big_questions.q: Electricity from a power station travels hundreds of kilometres along wires to your fan. Does it come back to the power station?
big_questions.hint: Every plug has at least two pins. Why do you think it needs more than one?

big_questions.q: Imagine a world with no electricity at all, not even in living things. Could anything in it be alive?
big_questions.hint: Your heart beats because of electrical signals. A touch-me-not folds their leaves because of one too.

story.title: Ammachi's Torch
story.note: The story is made up. Everything about the torch is true: two cells in a row only push together if they face the same way, and a crust on a spring can stop the electricity.
text: The rain came down on Kochi so hard that it drummed on the roof like a hundred fingers. Kavya was eight, and she was doing her sums at the dining table. Her little brother Arjun was building a tower of steel tumblers. Then, with a soft click, every light in the flat went out. The fan slowed down and stopped. The fridge went quiet.
"Power cut," said Ammachi, their grandmother, from the dark. "Kavya, there is a torch in the top drawer of my almirah. Bring it, mole."

Kavya felt her way along the wall to Ammachi's room. She found the drawer and the torch inside it. It was a heavy old torch made of silver metal, the kind that takes two fat cells. She pushed the switch forward. Nothing happened. She pushed it back and forward again. Still nothing.
"It doesn't work, Ammachi," she called.
"Then the cells must be finished," said Ammachi. "There are new ones in the kitchen, near the matchbox."

Kavya's mother lit a candle, and in its yellow light Kavya found two new cells. She unscrewed the bottom of the torch. The old cells slid out into her hand. She dropped in the two new ones and screwed the bottom back on. She pushed the switch.
Nothing.
Arjun giggled. "Your torch is broken."

Kavya did not giggle. She was thinking. That week, at her homeschool table, she had made a bulb light with one AA cell and a piece of wire. She knew the bulb only lit when the electricity had a whole path, from one end of the cell, through the bulb, and back to the other end. If there was a gap anywhere, the bulb stayed dark. So somewhere in this torch there was a gap.
"Amma, can I hold the candle close?" she asked. Her mother brought it over and sat beside her.

Kavya unscrewed the bottom again and tipped the cells out onto the table. She looked at them carefully. Each cell had a little bump at one end and a flat end at the other. The bump was the plus end. The flat end was the minus end.
"How did you put them in?" asked her mother.
"Bump first," said Kavya. Then she stopped. "No. The first one went in bump first. The second one I put in the other way, because it rolled."
"Does that matter?" asked Arjun.

Kavya thought about it. In a torch, the two cells sit in a line, one behind the other. Each cell pushes the electricity one way, from its minus end round to its plus end. "If they face the same way, they push together," she said slowly. "If one is turned round, it pushes back against the other one. Then they cancel out, and there is no push at all."
She put both cells in bump first, both facing the bulb. She screwed on the bottom and pushed the switch.
Still nothing.
Arjun opened his mouth, but his mother gave him a look, and he closed it again.

"There must be another gap," said Kavya. She tipped the cells out once more and peered into the bottom cap with the candle. At the bottom was the spring that presses the cells up towards the bulb. The spring was covered in a crust, white and greenish, like old chalk.
"What is that?" asked her mother.
"I think the old cells leaked," said Kavya. "That crust is not shiny metal. Maybe it doesn't let electricity through."

"Don't touch it with your fingers," said her mother. She brought an old toothbrush and a dry cloth. Carefully, Kavya scrubbed the spring until the silver metal showed again. Then her mother wiped the spring and the inside of the cap with the cloth, and they both washed their hands.
Kavya put the cells back in, both facing the bulb. She screwed the cap on tight. She held her breath and pushed the switch.
A circle of white light jumped onto the ceiling.
Arjun shouted, and his tower of tumblers fell over with a great clatter. Ammachi laughed from her room. "Who fixed it?"
"Kavya did," said her mother. "She found two gaps."

Kavya shone the torch round the room, onto the fallen tumblers, onto Arjun's surprised face, onto Ammachi's smile in the doorway. She was thinking about the electricity going round. Out of the cells, along the metal case of the torch, through the switch, into the bulb, and back down through the two cells and the clean spring. Round and round, in one loop, for as long as the switch was on.
Then the fan began to turn and the lights came back on. Kavya switched the torch off. She put it back in Ammachi's drawer with the cells facing the right way, ready for the next power cut.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a torch is one loop. The electricity goes from the cells, along the metal case, through the switch and the bulb, and back through the cells and the spring. Two cells in a row push together only when they face the same way. Turn one round, and the two pushes cancel. A leaked cell leaves a crust that is a poor conductor, so it made a gap in the loop at the spring. Kavya found both gaps because she knew the bulb needs a complete path.
ask: Why did the torch still not work after Kavya put in new cells?
What happened when one cell was turned the wrong way round? Why?
Why did the crust on the spring stop the torch from working?
Kavya's mother told her not to touch the crust. Why do you think she said that?
Can you trace the loop the electricity takes in a torch, using your finger on a drawing?

games.title: Close the Loop: a circuit card game
games.context: This is a card game. Each player builds a circuit on the table, card by card, from a cell, through a bulb and back to the cell. Insulator cards and Gap cards get in the way.

items.b: Water lets electricity through your skin
Opens and closes a gap in the circuit

items.f: What tiny particles move in a wire?
Do the electrons get used up in the bulb?
items.b: No, they go round and come back

rules: Shuffle the circuit cards and deal 5 to each player. Put the rest face down.
Your circuit must start at the + end of a CELL card, go through a BULB card, and come back to the − end of the same cell. The loop needs at least 3 cards besides the cell and the bulb.
On your turn, take one card. Then play one card on your circuit, or play a GAP! card on someone else's.
WIRE and CONDUCTOR cards join your loop. An INSULATOR card cannot be used as a wire. If you have to play one, put it aside.
A GAP! card breaks a circuit. That player must play a FIX IT card, or take the broken card out and replace it.

When your loop is complete, read the front of a question card and answer it. Turn the card over to check. Right? Your bulb lights: score 1 bulb and start a new circuit. Wrong? Try again on your next turn.
A SWITCH card in your loop protects it: a GAP! card played on you only opens the switch, and you can close it again on your next turn.
The first player to light 2 bulbs wins. Playing alone, try to light 2 bulbs in 15 turns.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Deal 5 cards each. 3. Each player puts a CELL card in front of them, if they have one.
flow.say: Each of us is going to build a circuit, card by card. It must go from the cell, through a bulb, and all the way back.
flow.kid: Take 5 cards. Put a cell in front of you. Build a loop to a bulb and back!
flow.context: This is the first step of Close the Loop, a card game where you build circuits.

flow.do: Play one practice turn together.
flow.say: Practice turn. I have a wooden stick card. Can I use it as part of my loop?
flow.kid: Practice turn. Can a wooden stick card join your loop? Tap your answer.

check.q: Can a wooden stick card join your loop like a wire?
options: Yes, any card can join the loop
No, wood is an insulator, so it makes a gap
check.why: Wood does not let electricity through, so it would leave a gap in the loop and the bulb would stay dark. Only wire cards and conductor cards, which are metals, can join the loop.

flow.do: 1. Take turns: take a card, play a card. 2. When a loop is complete, read a question card. 3. Keep score on the sheet.
flow.say: Take a card and play a card. Watch out for GAP! cards. When your loop is complete, answer a question to light your bulb.
flow.kid: Take a card. Play a card. Loop complete? Answer a question to light it!
flow.parent: Before each player's bulb lights, ask them to trace the loop with a finger from + round to −. If they find a gap, they must fix it first. The game is quicker with fewer GAP! cards for younger players.

flow.do: Finish and talk about the switch card.
flow.say: Why did the switch card protect your circuit? What does a real switch do?
flow.kid: Why did the switch card help you? What does a real switch do?
flow.think: Is a switch a gap, or a bridge? Or both?

games.context: This is a quick game about electrical safety. A grown-up reads a situation, and you hold up a green card for safe or a red card for danger, then say why.

printables.title: One green SAFE card and one red DANGER card for each player

rules: Each player has a green SAFE card and a red DANGER card.
A grown-up reads a situation card aloud. Everyone holds up SAFE or DANGER at the same time.
Each player who is right scores 1 point. Say why, and score 1 more point.
Playing alone, read each card yourself and check the answer in the brackets.

flow.do: Hand out the cards and read the first situation.
flow.say: Listen carefully. Then hold up green for safe or red for danger. Meenakshi tests a steel spoon with an AA cell and a bulb.
flow.kid: Hold up green for safe. Red for danger. Ready?
flow.context: This is the start of Safe or Danger?, a quick game about staying safe with electricity.

flow.do: Read the cards one at a time. After each one, ask for the reason.
flow.say: Why is that dangerous? What could happen?
flow.kid: Safe or danger? Hold up your card. Then say why.

check.q: Lakshmi switches on the fan with wet hands after her bath. Safe or danger?
options: Safe, because the switch is plastic
Danger, because water lets electricity through her skin much more easily
check.why: Wet skin lets electricity through far more easily than dry skin. Water can also get inside the switch. So always dry your hands first. Picking 'safe' is a good thought, because the switch cover is plastic, an insulator. But water can carry electricity past the plastic.

flow.do: Talk about the AA cell card.
flow.say: Priya touched both ends of an AA cell, and that was safe. But a wall socket is never safe. What is the difference?
flow.kid: An AA cell is safe to touch. A socket is not. Why?
flow.parent: An AA cell pushes at 1.5 volts, too weakly to push enough electricity through dry skin for you to notice. A wall socket in India pushes at 230 volts, about 150 times as hard. That is strong enough to push electricity through a body.

setup.caption: 2. Say why it is safe or dangerous.

experiments.title: The Conductor Test: which things complete the circuit?
experiments.question: Which everyday things let electricity through, so that the bulb lights, and which things stop it?
experiments.predict: Look at the things on the table. Guess which ones will make the bulb light. Put them in two piles. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same cell, the same bulb and the same wires for every object. Touch both wire ends firmly to the object, about 2 cm apart. Only the object changes. Test each object twice, because a loose touch can fool you.

materials.item: an AA cell, 1.5 volts, in a single AA cell holder with two wires. No holder? Tape the wires to the cell's two ends with cello tape.
a small torch bulb marked 1.5 V or 2.5 V, in a bulb holder. An LED will not light from one AA cell.
plastic-covered wire, about 20 cm long, with 2 cm of bare copper at each end. Or a strip of aluminium foil folded lengthwise four times.

about 12 things to test: a steel spoon, a coin, a plain steel paper clip, a plastic-coated paper clip, a strip of aluminium foil, a steel key, a wooden ice-cream stick, a plastic ruler, a rubber band or eraser, a sheet of paper, a cotton cloth, a glass bangle
a pencil sharpened at both ends, or a piece of thick pencil lead
cello tape

experiments.safety: Use only AA cells, never a wall socket or a charger. Never join the two ends of a cell with just a wire or foil, because the wire gets hot. A grown-up strips the wire ends and stays close.

schedule.what: Build a circuit tester with a gap. Guess, then test 12 things. Sort them into conductors and insulators.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw two big circles, one for conductors and one for insulators, and write each object in the right circle.

flow.do: 1. Join one wire from the cell holder to the bulb holder. 2. Join a second wire to the other side of the bulb holder. 3. Leave the free ends of the cell wire and the bulb wire apart. 4. Touch the two free ends together.
flow.say: First we build a tester. It is a circuit with a gap in it. Watch what happens when I touch the two loose ends together.
flow.kid: Build a circuit with one gap. Touch the two loose ends together. Does the bulb light?
flow.parent: The bulb should light when the two bare ends touch, and go out when they part. If it does not light, check that the bulb is screwed in firmly and the bare copper is touching. A 2.5 volt bulb glows dimly on one cell, so close the curtains. If your tester never lights, try a fresh cell.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Conductor Test. Here you build a circuit tester: a circuit with a gap, which lights when something joins the gap.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the 12 things. 2. Ask your child to put them in two piles: 'will light' and 'won't light'. 3. Ask for a reason for each pile. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: The gap is like a bridge that is missing. Which of these things will carry the electricity across it? Make two piles. Why did you put each one there?
flow.kid: Make two piles. Will light. Won't light. Why did you choose that pile?

ask.q: Why do you think the spoon will light the bulb?
good: Because electricity goes through metal, like in a wire.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Any reason is good if your child says it. The reasons tell you what they think now.

flow.do: 1. Press both bare wire ends firmly onto the first object, about 2 cm apart. 2. Look at the bulb. 3. Write the answer. 4. Try again, then go on to the next object.
flow.say: Let's test them one at a time. Press both ends on firmly. Watch the bulb closely. A dim glow counts too.
flow.kid: Press both wire ends onto the object. Look at the bulb. Write yes or no. Try it twice.
flow.parent: The steel spoon, coin, plain paper clip, foil and key should light the bulb brightly. The wood, plastic, rubber, paper, cloth and glass should not. The coated paper clip will not light it until you scrape the plastic off each end. For the pencil, touch one wire to the lead at each sharpened end. The bulb may glow only very dimly, or not at all, because graphite conducts much less well than metal. If it does not glow, try a short piece of lead, about 2 cm, between the two wire ends.

flow.do: Look at the coated paper clip result together.
flow.say: The plain clip lit the bulb, but the coloured clip did not. Both are steel inside. Why do you think that happened?
flow.kid: The plain clip lit the bulb. The coloured clip did not. Why?

check.q: A paper clip with a plastic coat does not light the bulb. Why?
options: The steel inside is too thin
The plastic coat is an insulator, so the electricity cannot reach the steel
Coloured things never conduct
check.why: The plastic coat is an insulator. The wire ends touch only plastic, so the electricity cannot reach the steel inside. Scrape a little plastic off each end, and the clip lights the bulb. Picking 'too thin' is a fair guess, but the plain clip is just as thin and it works. Colour has nothing to do with it.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: metal things let electricity through, and other things stop it. What I saw: the spoon, the coin, the key and the foil lit the bulb. The wood, plastic, paper and glass did not. Why: metals let electricity through, so they are conductors. The others do not, so they are insulators. That is why wires are copper inside plastic.

check.q: Which group were nearly all the conductors in?
options: Shiny things
Metals
Heavy things
check.why: Nearly all the conductors were metals: steel, copper, aluminium and brass. Pencil graphite is the odd one out, a conductor that is not a metal. Picking 'shiny things' is a good try at a pattern. But a glass bangle is shiny and does not conduct, and a dull steel key does.

experiments.context: In this experiment you build a circuit tester and use it to find out which things let electricity through. You test spoons, coins, paper clips, wood, plastic and more.

experiments.title: Where Is the Gap? Breaking the loop in different places
experiments.question: Does it matter where the gap in a circuit is? And does a very long wire make the bulb light later?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If you break the loop far away from the bulb, will the bulb still glow a little? With a very long wire, will the bulb light at once, or a moment later? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same cell, bulb and wires each time. Only the place of the gap changes. Then only the length of one wire changes. Try each one three times.

materials.item: an AA cell, 1.5 volts, in a single AA cell holder with two wires. No holder? Tape the wires to the cell's two ends with cello tape.
a small torch bulb marked 1.5 V or 2.5 V, in a bulb holder. An LED will not light from one AA cell.
plastic-covered wire, about 20 cm long, with 2 cm of bare copper at each end. Or a strip of aluminium foil folded lengthwise four times.
a long wire, about 2 metres, with bare ends. Or 15 plain steel paper clips hooked into a chain.

experiments.safety: Use only AA cells, never a wall socket or a charger. Never join the two ends of a cell with just a wire or foil, because the wire gets hot. A grown-up strips the wire ends and stays close.

schedule.what: Break a complete circuit in three places. Then add a very long wire and watch when the bulb lights.

experiments.record: Draw the loop three times. Mark where you made the gap each time, and draw the bulb lit or dark.

flow.do: 1. Make a complete circuit with the cell, the bulb and three wires. 2. Twist the wire ends together firmly where they join. 3. Check that the bulb lights.
flow.say: Here is a complete loop. Trace the path with your finger, from the cell, through the bulb and back to the cell.
flow.kid: Build a full loop. Trace it with your finger. Cell, bulb, back to the cell.
flow.context: This is the first step of Where Is the Gap? Here you build a complete loop with three wires, ready to break it in different places.

flow.do: 1. Untwist the join next to the plus end of the cell. 2. Join it again. 3. Untwist the join on the far side of the bulb. 4. Join it again. 5. Untwist the join in the middle of the loop.
flow.say: We will make a gap in three places. Before each one, tell me: will the bulb go out, or glow a little?
flow.kid: Make a gap next to the cell. Then after the bulb. Then in the middle. Guess first each time.
flow.parent: The bulb goes out completely and at once, wherever the gap is. Many children expect the electricity on the cell's side of the gap to keep the bulb glowing a little, or expect a gap after the bulb not to matter.

check.q: You make a gap after the bulb, on the way back to the cell. What happens?
options: The bulb stays lit, because the electricity has already passed it
The bulb goes out, because the loop is broken
The bulb glows half as bright
check.why: The bulb goes out. Electricity flows only while the whole loop is complete, all the way back to the cell. A gap anywhere stops the flow everywhere. Picking 'stays lit' means thinking that electricity goes from the cell into the bulb and stops there. It actually goes round and back.

flow.do: 1. Take out one short wire. 2. Put the 2 metre wire, or the paper clip chain, in its place. 3. Hold one end of it off the cell. 4. Watch the bulb closely, and touch the end on.
flow.say: Now one wire is very long. When I touch it on, will the bulb light at once? Or will it wait for the electricity to get there?
flow.kid: Now one wire is very long. Watch the bulb. Does it light at once? Or later?
flow.parent: The bulb lights at once, with no delay you can see. With a paper clip chain it may be a little dimmer, because each join between clips lets the electricity through less well. That is fine. What matters is that there is no wait.

ask.q: Why do you think the bulb lit straight away?
good: The electricity was already in the wire.
The whole loop starts moving at once.

flow.do: Talk about the cycle chain. Then ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Think of a cycle chain. Push the pedal, and every link moves at once, even the far ones. Electrons in a wire are like that. Now tell me what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.kid: Think of a cycle chain. Every link moves at once. Now say: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a gap anywhere stops the bulb, and a long wire does not make it wait. What I saw: the bulb went out every time, wherever I made the gap. With the 2 metre wire it still lit at once. Why: the tiny electrons are already in the wire all the way round. The cell pushes them all together, like a cycle chain. So a break anywhere stops them all.
flow.think: If the electrons go round and come back to the cell, what is the cell running out of when it goes flat?

experiments.context: In this experiment you break a working circuit in different places, and test a very long wire. You find out whether the place of the gap matters, and whether electricity takes time to arrive.

experiments.title: Two Cells: brighter, or nothing at all?
experiments.question: What happens to the bulb when you add a second cell? And what happens if the second cell faces the wrong way?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will two cells make the bulb brighter, the same, or dimmer? And what if one cell is turned round? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bulb and wires each time. Only the cells change. Look at the bulb in the same light each time, and compare it with the one-cell bulb.

materials.item: two AA cells, each in a single AA cell holder with wires
a 2.5 V torch bulb in a bulb holder
plastic-covered wire, about 20 cm long, with 2 cm of bare copper at each end. Or a strip of aluminium foil folded lengthwise four times.

experiments.safety: Use only AA cells, never a wall socket or a charger. Never join the two ends of a cell with just a wire or foil, because the wire gets hot. A grown-up strips the wire ends and stays close. Use no more than two AA cells with a torch bulb, or the bulb may burn out.

schedule.what: Light a bulb with one cell, then two cells facing the same way, then two cells facing opposite ways.

experiments.record: Draw the bulb three times. Draw lines around it to show how bright it was.

flow.do: 1. Light the bulb with one cell. 2. Look at how bright it is.
flow.say: Here is our bulb with one cell. Remember how bright it looks.
flow.kid: Light the bulb with one cell. Remember how bright it is.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Cells. Here you light a bulb with one cell, so you can compare it with two cells later.

flow.do: 1. Join the red wire of one holder to the black wire of the other holder. 2. Join the two free wires to the bulb. 3. Compare the brightness.
flow.say: Now two cells are in a row, both facing the same way. Will the bulb be brighter, the same or dimmer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Join two cells in a row, plus to minus. Guess first. Brighter or dimmer?
flow.parent: The bulb is clearly brighter, because two cells in a row push twice as hard, 3 volts instead of 1.5 volts. Red wires usually come from the plus end and black from the minus end. Check yours.

flow.do: 1. Take one cell out of its holder and put it back the other way round. 2. Look at the bulb. 3. If the turned cell does not touch at both ends, put it back the right way. Then join the red wire to the red wire, and the two black wires to the bulb.
flow.say: Now one cell faces the wrong way. What will happen this time? Why?
flow.kid: Turn one cell round. Now what does the bulb do?
flow.parent: The bulb does not light, or glows only faintly. Each cell pushes the electricity one way round the loop. Turned round, the two pushes are against each other and cancel out. This is the mistake Kavya made in the story.

check.q: Two cells face opposite ways, and the bulb does not light. Why?
options: The cells are both flat
The two cells push opposite ways round the loop, so their pushes cancel
Two cells are too strong for the bulb
check.why: Each cell pushes the electricity one way round the loop. When one is turned round, the two pushes are equal and opposite, and they cancel. Turn it back, and the bulb shines brighter than with one cell. Picking 'both flat' is a sensible guess, but the same cells lit the bulb a minute ago.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Now tell me what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: two cells facing the same way make the bulb brighter, and two facing opposite ways cancel out. What I saw: the bulb was brighter with two cells in a row. When I turned one round, it went dark. Why: each cell pushes the electricity round the loop, and two pushes the same way add up.

experiments.context: In this experiment you find out what a second cell does to a bulb, and what happens when one cell is put in the wrong way round.

materials.item: one loose AA cell, 1.5 volts, out of any holder
a small torch bulb marked 1.5 V or 2.5 V, out of its holder
one wire, about 15 cm long, with bare ends. Or a strip of aluminium foil folded lengthwise four times.
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Use only an AA cell. Do not hold the wire across both ends of the cell for long with no bulb, because it gets hot. A grown-up stays close.

schedule.what: Try to light a bulb with one cell and one wire. Draw every try.

activities.record: Draw each try. Put a tick by the ones that lit and a cross by the ones that did not.

flow.do: 1. Give your child the cell, the bulb and the wire. 2. Say the challenge. 3. Let them try for at least five minutes before helping.
flow.say: Here is a challenge. Can you make this bulb light with just these three things? Before you try, show me how you think they go together.
flow.kid: Can you light the bulb? You have one cell, one wire, one bulb. Try lots of ways.
flow.parent: Most children first touch the wire to one end of the cell and the bulb to the other, or stand the bulb on the cell with the wire to its tip. Neither works. Let them try. The struggle is what makes the answer stick. If the room is bright, a 2.5 volt bulb's glow can be hard to see, so dim the lights.
flow.context: This is a starting challenge for the circuits unit. You try to light a bulb with one cell and one wire, and find out what a bulb needs.

flow.do: If they are stuck, give one hint: the bulb has two metal contacts, the tip and the side.
flow.say: Look at the bulb closely. Where is the metal? The bulb has two metal parts. What if each one touched a different end of the cell?
flow.kid: Look at the bulb. Find two metal parts. The tip and the side.
flow.parent: The way that works: stand the bulb's tip on the bump at the top of the cell. Then hold one end of the wire on the bulb's metal side and the other end on the flat bottom of the cell. There are other ways too, such as the wire from the bump to the bulb's side, and the bulb's tip on the flat end.

flow.do: Look at the drawings together and talk about the ones that lit.
flow.say: What do all the tries that lit have in common? Trace the path with your finger.
flow.kid: Look at your ticks. What is the same in all of them?

options: Bulb tip on the top of the cell, no wire
Bulb tip on the top of the cell, and a wire from the bulb's side to the bottom of the cell
Wire from the top of the cell to the bulb's tip, nothing else
check.why: The electricity needs a full loop: out of one end of the cell, through the bulb, and back to the other end. The bulb's tip and side are the way in and the way out. Picking the first or third answer means only one end of the cell is joined to the bulb, so there is no way back.

flow.think: Why does the electricity need to get back to the cell?

activities.context: This is a quick challenge to start the unit. You try to light a bulb with one cell and one wire, and find out that electricity needs a full loop.

activities.title: Electricity Hunt: wall or cell?

materials.item: a big sheet of paper and a pencil
coloured pencils or crayons

activities.safety: Look at sockets, plugs and wires, but do not touch them. Only grown-ups plug things in or switch them off at the socket.

schedule.what: Walk round the home and list everything that uses electricity. Sort the list into mains and cells, and by what each thing makes.

activities.record: Make a chart with two big columns, 'Plugged into the wall' and 'Runs on cells'. Draw a small sign by each one: a sun for light, a note for sound, a flame for heat, a snowflake for cold, an arrow for movement.

flow.do: 1. Draw the two columns. 2. Ask your child to guess how many things in the home use electricity.
flow.say: How many things in our home do you think use electricity? Make a guess. Then we will count.
flow.kid: Guess how many things at home use electricity. Then we count!
flow.context: This is the start of the Electricity Hunt. You find every electrical thing in your home and sort them.

flow.do: 1. Walk through each room together. 2. Your child writes or draws each thing in the right column. 3. Look for a wire and plug, or a place for cells.
flow.say: Look for a wire and a plug. That means it uses mains electricity from the wall. Look for a little door for cells. That means it runs on cells.
flow.kid: Walk round your home. Find a plug? Write it under 'wall'. Find cells? Write it under 'cells'.
flow.parent: Typical finds: fan, tube light, fridge, mixer-grinder, TV, iron, geyser, washing machine, water pump, Wi-Fi box and phone charger use the mains. A TV remote, wall clock, torch, toy car, weighing scale and kitchen timer use cells. A phone and a laptop have their own batteries that are charged from the mains. They can go in both columns.

flow.do: Look at the chart and add the signs for what each thing makes.
flow.say: Now let's add a sign for what each thing makes: light, sound, heat, cold or movement. Which ones make two things?
flow.kid: Draw a sign by each thing. Light, sound, heat, cold or movement?

check.q: Which of these would keep working in a power cut, without an inverter?
options: The ceiling fan
The wall clock with an AA cell
The fridge
check.why: The wall clock runs on its own cell, so it does not need the mains. The fan and the fridge are plugged into the wall, so they stop when the power goes off. Picking the fridge is natural, because it stays cold for a while. But its motor stops at once.

flow.think: Which column is safe for experiments? Why?

activities.context: In this activity you hunt for everything in your home that uses electricity. You sort them into things that plug into the wall and things that run on cells.

activities.title: Spot the Danger: a safety walk

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a sheet of paper for a safety poster

activities.safety: This is a walk for looking only. Nobody touches a socket, a plug or a wire during it.

schedule.what: Walk round the home with a grown-up and find places where electricity needs care. Write the rules.

activities.record: Write five safety rules, each with its reason. Make them into a poster for the fridge.

flow.do: Sit down together before the walk and say the first rule.
flow.say: The electricity in our wall sockets is 230 volts. That is about 150 times as strong as an AA cell. It can push electricity through a person and kill them. So the first rule is: only grown-ups plug in and unplug things.
flow.kid: Wall sockets are very strong. They can kill. Only grown-ups plug things in.
flow.context: This is the start of a safety walk. You learn the electricity rules by looking for places in your home where electricity needs care.

flow.do: 1. Walk to the kitchen, the bathroom and near any extension board. 2. At each place, ask what could go wrong. 3. Your child writes a rule.
flow.say: Look at this socket by the sink. What could go wrong here? Why is water a problem near electricity?
flow.kid: Look carefully. What could go wrong here? Write a rule.
flow.parent: Good rules with reasons. Never touch switches or plugs with wet hands, because water lets electricity through your skin more easily. Never push anything into a socket. Never pull a plug out by its wire, because the wire can break inside. Stay away from wires with cracked plastic, because bare copper can give a shock. Never fly kites near power lines. Keep button cells away from babies, because a swallowed one burns.

flow.do: Read the rules back and check one with a question.
flow.say: Here is a question. Why do you think wires have plastic around them?
flow.kid: Why do wires have plastic around them? Tap your answer.

check.q: Why is there plastic around the copper in a fan's wire?
options: To make it look nice
Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps the electricity inside the copper and away from us
To make the electricity go faster
check.why: Plastic does not let electricity through. It keeps the electricity in the copper and stops it reaching our hands. That is why a wire with cracked plastic is dangerous. Picking 'look nice' is partly true, because wires come in colours. But the colours have a job too: they tell electricians which wire is which.

activities.context: In this activity you go on a safety walk around your home with a grown-up and write rules for staying safe with electricity.

activities.title: Inside a Torch

materials.item: a torch that takes AA or D cells and comes apart by unscrewing. An LED torch is fine.
a cloth to lay the parts on

activities.safety: Do not take apart a torch with a battery you cannot take out, such as a charging torch. If you see white crust on the cells or spring, a grown-up wipes it off with a dry cloth and everyone washes their hands.

schedule.what: Take a torch apart, find its circuit, and put it back together.

activities.record: Draw the torch parts and draw a line showing the loop the electricity takes.

flow.do: 1. Unscrew the torch over the cloth. 2. Lay out the parts in order: cells, spring, case, switch, bulb or LED, reflector.
flow.say: A torch is a circuit hidden inside a case. Let's take it apart and find the loop.
flow.kid: Unscrew the torch. Lay out all the parts on the cloth.
flow.context: In this activity you take a torch apart and find the circuit inside it.

flow.do: Point to each part and ask whether it is a conductor or an insulator.
flow.say: Which parts are metal, and which are plastic? Which parts do you think the electricity goes through?
flow.kid: Which parts are metal? Which are plastic? Where does electricity go?

ask.q: Why is the spring made of metal?
good: So the electricity can go through it.
It is a conductor, and it pushes the cells against the bulb.

flow.parent: In most torches the loop goes from the cells through the spring, along a metal strip or the metal case, through the switch, into the bulb or LED, and back into the top of the cells. The plastic case, or the rubber grip, is an insulator.

flow.do: 1. Put the torch back together. 2. Switch it on and off. 3. Your child traces the loop on their drawing.
flow.say: Put it back together and switch it on. What does the switch do to the loop?
flow.kid: Put it back. Switch it on and off. What does the switch do?

check.q: What happens inside a torch when you slide the switch off?
options: The cells stop making electricity forever
Two metal parts move apart, making a gap in the loop
The bulb takes all the electricity out
check.why: Sliding the switch off moves two metal parts apart. The air gap between them is an insulator, so the loop is broken and the flow stops. The cells keep their stored energy until you switch on again. Picking 'stop forever' is not right, because switching on again lights the torch at once.

activities.context: In this activity you take a torch apart and trace the hidden loop that lights it.

setup.caption: 1. Take the torch apart. Lay out the parts.

activities.title: Make a Paper Clip Switch

materials.item: an AA cell, 1.5 volts, in a single AA cell holder with two wires. No holder? Tape the wires to the cell's two ends with cello tape.
a small torch bulb marked 1.5 V or 2.5 V, in a bulb holder. An LED will not light from one AA cell.
plastic-covered wire, about 20 cm long, with 2 cm of bare copper at each end. Or a strip of aluminium foil folded lengthwise four times.
two drawing pins and a plain steel paper clip
a piece of thick cardboard, about 10 cm square

activities.safety: Drawing pins are sharp. A grown-up pushes them in. Use only AA cells, never a wall socket or a charger. Never join the two ends of a cell with just a wire or foil, because the wire gets hot. A grown-up strips the wire ends and stays close.

schedule.what: Make a switch from drawing pins and a paper clip. Put it in a circuit and use it.

activities.record: Draw your circuit with the switch open and closed. Draw the bulb dark and lit.

flow.do: 1. Wrap the bare end of one wire round the spike of a drawing pin. 2. Push the pin into the cardboard, so its head presses the wire down. 3. Do the same with the second wire and pin, about 2 cm away. 4. Hook the paper clip round one pin.
flow.say: We are making a switch. It is just a gap we can open and close. The paper clip is the bridge across the gap.
flow.kid: Wrap a wire round each pin. Push the pins in, 2 cm apart. Hook a paper clip on one.
flow.context: In this activity you make your own switch from two drawing pins and a paper clip, and use it to turn a bulb on and off.

flow.do: 1. Join the switch into the circuit, between the cell and the bulb. 2. Swing the paper clip onto the second pin. 3. Swing it off again.
flow.say: Swing the clip across. What happens? Now swing it away. Why does the bulb go out?
flow.kid: Swing the clip onto the other pin. Light! Swing it away. Dark!
flow.parent: If the bulb does not light with the clip closed, press the clip down firmly on the pin. Shiny drawing pins work best. Painted ones may need the paint scraped off.

flow.do: Ask why the switch is on cardboard and not on a steel plate.
flow.say: Why did we put the switch on cardboard? What would happen on a steel plate?
flow.kid: Why cardboard? What if the switch was on a steel plate?

check.q: Why is the paper clip switch built on cardboard?
options: Cardboard is an insulator, so the electricity can only cross the gap through the clip
Cardboard is a conductor
Cardboard is lighter than steel
check.why: Cardboard is an insulator. With the clip away, nothing can carry the electricity across the gap, so the bulb is off. On a steel plate, the steel would join the two pins, and the bulb would stay on all the time. Picking 'lighter' is true, but it is not the reason.

flow.do: Your child sends a message with flashes: one flash for yes, two flashes for no.
flow.say: Can you send me a message with flashes? One flash for yes and two flashes for no. Is it raining today?
flow.kid: Send a message with your switch. One flash means yes. Two means no.
flow.think: Your switch was a gap you could open and close. Where else in the home is there a gap like that?

activities.context: In this activity you make a switch from a paper clip, and use it to open and close a circuit.

setup.art: Two shiny drawing pins in a square of cardboard, 2 cm apart, a paper clip hooked on one of them, and a wire wrapped under each pin.
setup.caption: 1. Two pins and a paper clip on cardboard.

setup.art: The switch joined into a circuit with a cell and a bulb, the clip swung across both pins and the bulb glowing.
setup.caption: 2. Close the switch, and the bulb lights.

activities.title: Be the Circuit: a string loop

materials.item: a long piece of string or a dupatta, about 4 metres, tied into a loop
3 or more people

activities.safety: Hold the string loosely. Do not wrap it round fingers or necks.

schedule.what: Act out a circuit with a loop of string. One person is the cell, one is the bulb.

activities.record: Draw the loop of people, with arrows for which way the string moved.

flow.do: 1. Everyone stands in a circle holding the string loop loosely. 2. One person is the cell. 3. One person is the bulb, and holds the string very lightly so it rubs their hands.
flow.say: The string is like the electrons in a wire. They are already there, all the way round. The cell pulls the string round. Let's see what the bulb feels.
flow.kid: Stand in a circle. Hold the string loosely. Who is the cell? Who is the bulb?
flow.context: In this activity you act out a circuit with a loop of string. It shows how the electrons move round a wire all at once.

flow.do: 1. The cell pulls the string steadily, hand over hand. 2. The bulb says 'warm' when they feel the string rubbing. 3. Then one person lets go and drops their part of the loop.
flow.say: Bulb, tell us when you feel the string start to rub. Did you feel it at once? Now someone let go and drop the string. What happens to the bulb?
flow.kid: Cell, pull the string round. Bulb, can you feel it rub? Now drop it!
flow.parent: The bulb feels the string move at the same moment the cell starts pulling, even though no part of the string moved far. The rubbing on the bulb's hands is like the filament getting hot. When someone drops the string, the cell can no longer pull it round, and the bulb feels nothing. That is a broken circuit.

flow.do: Talk about what the model shows and what it does not.
flow.say: Did the string get used up in the bulb's hands? What did the cell use up, pulling it round?
flow.kid: Was the string used up? What did the cell use up?

check.q: In the string model, what is the cell using up?
options: The string
Its own energy, from pulling
The bulb
check.why: The string goes round and comes back, just like electrons in a wire. The cell uses up its energy pulling it. A real cell uses up the energy stored in its chemicals. Picking 'the string' is the common idea that a cell is full of electricity that gets used up. The string, like the electrons, is still all there.

flow.think: Every model leaves something out. What is different about real electrons and our string?

activities.context: In this act-out you make a circuit from people and a loop of string, to see why a bulb lights at once and why a break anywhere stops it.

projects.title: Light Up a Shoebox Room

materials.item: an AA cell, 1.5 volts, in a single AA cell holder with two wires. No holder? Tape the wires to the cell's two ends with cello tape.
a second AA cell in a holder, to make the light brighter
a small torch bulb marked 1.5 V or 2.5 V, in a bulb holder. An LED will not light from one AA cell.
plastic-covered wire, about 2 metres in all, cut into pieces
a paper clip switch, from the switch activity
a shoebox, coloured paper, glue, scissors and cello tape

projects.safety: Scissors and drawing pins: a grown-up helps. Use only AA cells, never a wall socket or a charger. Never join the two ends of a cell with just a wire or foil, because the wire gets hot. A grown-up strips the wire ends and stays close. Switch the light off when you finish, so the cells do not run down.

schedule.what: Decorate a shoebox as a room. Plan where the light and the switch go, and draw the circuit.
Fix the bulb in the roof and the switch on the outside wall. Join the circuit and test it.

projects.record: Draw the circuit plan before you build it. After building, write what you changed and why.

flow.do: 1. Turn the shoebox on its side to make a room. 2. Decorate it with paper: a kolam on the floor, a window, a bed. 3. Draw a plan of the circuit. Show the cell, the switch, the bulb and the wires joining them in a loop.
flow.say: We are going to light up a room, like a real electrician. Electricians draw a plan first. Where will the light go? Where will the switch be?
flow.kid: Make a room in a shoebox. Draw a plan. Where do the bulb, switch and cell go?
flow.context: This is the first day of a 2-day project. You decorate a shoebox room, then wire a real light and switch into it.

flow.do: 1. Make a small hole in the roof and push the bulb holder's wires through. 2. Fix the switch on the outside wall with tape. 3. Join the cell, the switch and the bulb in one loop. 4. Test it, find any gaps and fix them.
flow.say: Now we follow the plan. If it doesn't light, we hunt for the gap, the way Kavya did with the torch.
flow.kid: Fix the bulb in the roof. Put the switch outside. Join the loop. Does it light?
flow.wait: Day 2: build and test the circuit.
flow.parent: Most problems are loose joins. Twist bare wire ends together tightly and wrap them in tape. If the light is dim and your bulb is marked 2.5 V, join a second cell in a row, plus to minus. A 1.5 V bulb may burn out on two cells.

check.q: Your shoebox light does not come on when you close the switch. What do you check first?
options: Buy a new bulb
Follow the loop with your finger and look for a loose join or gap
Add more tape everywhere
check.why: Most circuits that do not work have a gap, usually a loose join. Following the loop from + round to − finds it. A new bulb is only needed if the filament is broken. Tape helps hold joins, but tape over a gap does not close it, because tape is an insulator.

projects.context: In this 2-day project you wire a real light and switch into a shoebox room.

challenges.title: The Steady Hand Game
challenges.problem: Make a game that tests how steady your hand is. A wand must move along a path without touching it. If it touches, a bulb lights up.
constraints: Use only AA cells, a bulb, wire, foil and things from home.
The bulb must light only when the wand touches the path.
The path must have at least three bends.
materials: an AA cell in a holder and a bulb in a holder
a strip of thick cardboard about 30 cm long
a plain steel paper clip, opened into a small loop on a stick
general: Cut a wavy path in the cardboard and cover its edges with foil. Join the foil to the cell. Join the paper clip loop to the bulb. When the loop touches the foil, the circuit is complete.
Bend a thick piece of bare wire into a wavy shape, like the games at a mela, and use a loop of wire as the wand.
creative: Put a small foil 'safe' pad at each end, where the wand can rest without scoring.
Use two paths, a wide one for younger children and a narrow one for experts.
Count the flashes as penalty points.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own steady hand game. Draw it, build it, and challenge your family.

flow.do: Look at the problem together and draw two ideas.
flow.say: When the wand touches the path, the bulb must light. So the wand and the path are two ends of a gap. Let's draw two ideas.
flow.kid: The wand and the path are the two ends of a gap. Draw two ideas.
flow.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a game that lights a bulb when your hand shakes.

flow.do: 1. Cut a wavy path in the cardboard. 2. Cover the edge with foil. 3. Join one wire from the cell to the foil, and tape it. 4. Join the bulb to the cell. 5. Join the bulb's other wire to the paper clip wand.
flow.say: Build the path and the wand. Then touch the wand to the foil to check that the bulb lights.
flow.kid: Build the foil path. Join the wand. Touch the foil. Does it light?
flow.parent: The foil must be in one unbroken piece, or overlapping pieces pressed together, so the whole path is joined to the cell. The wand's handle should be a pencil or stick, an insulator, so you hold it there.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. 2. Improve it and play again. 3. Read the usual and creative ideas.
flow.say: Play it. What could make it harder? Here are some other ideas. Can you invent a better one?
flow.kid: Play it. Make it harder. Can you invent a better one?

check.q: Why does the bulb light only when the wand touches the foil?
options: The wand and the foil are the two sides of a gap. Touching closes the circuit
The foil makes electricity
The bulb senses your hand shaking
check.why: The wand and the foil are both joined into the circuit, with a gap between them. When they touch, the gap closes and the bulb lights. It is a switch that your shaky hand closes. Picking 'foil makes electricity' is not right, because only the cell pushes the electricity.

setup.caption: 1. Build a foil path and a wand.

setup.art: A child moving the wand carefully along the path, and the bulb flashing as the loop touches the foil.

challenges.title: The Step-On Light
challenges.problem: Make a switch that turns a light on when someone steps on it, like a doormat that lights up when a visitor arrives.
constraints: Use only AA cells, a bulb, wire, foil and things from home.
The light must be off until someone presses, and go off again when they let go.
It must work 10 times in a row.
materials: an AA cell in a holder and a bulb in a holder
two pieces of cardboard about 15 cm square
a kitchen sponge or a folded piece of thick cloth, with a hole cut in the middle
general: Stick foil on one side of each piece of cardboard. Put the sponge with a hole between them, foil sides facing. When you press, the two foils touch through the hole.
Use a strip of folded card as a springy hinge that keeps the two foils apart until pressed.
creative: Make the light come on when a box lid is opened instead of pressed.
Hide it under a rug to catch someone sneaking into the room.
Put two step-on switches at two doors, so either one lights the bulb.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own press switch. Where in your home would it be useful?

flow.do: Talk about press switches in the home, such as the doorbell and the light in a fridge.
flow.say: The fridge light comes on when you open the door. The doorbell rings only while you press. These are press switches. Let's make one you can step on.
flow.kid: A doorbell is a press switch. Let's make one you can step on!
flow.context: This is an engineering challenge. You make a press switch that lights a bulb when someone steps on it.

flow.do: 1. Cover one side of each cardboard square with foil. 2. Tape a wire to each foil. 3. Put the sponge with a hole between the foils. 4. Tape the edges. 5. Join the wires into the circuit with the cell and bulb.
flow.say: When you press, the two foils touch through the hole and close the gap. When you let go, the sponge pushes them apart.
flow.kid: Make two foil squares. Put the sponge between them. Press. Does it light?
flow.parent: If the light stays on, the hole is too big or the sponge too thin. If it never lights, make the hole bigger. Test it by pressing with a hand before stepping on it in socks.

flow.do: 1. Step on it 10 times. 2. Improve it. 3. Read the usual and creative ideas.
flow.say: Does it work 10 times in a row? What could make it better?
flow.kid: Step on it 10 times. Does it work every time? Make it better.

check.q: Why does the sponge need a hole in it?
options: So the two foils can touch through it when pressed, and close the circuit
To make it lighter
So the electricity can be stored in the hole
check.why: The sponge is an insulator that keeps the foils apart. The hole lets the foils touch only when you press. Then the gap closes and the bulb lights. Let go, and the sponge pushes them apart again. Picking 'stored in the hole' is not right, because electricity is not stored in a switch.
