quiz.p: Which of these runs on mains electricity from the wall?
quiz.why: A mixer-grinder has a wire and a plug, so it uses mains electricity. The remote, the clock and the torch run on cells. Picking the clock is easy to do, because some big clocks are plugged in, but most wall clocks use one AA cell.

quiz.p: Why must you never touch a switch with wet hands?
opts: Water lets electricity through your skin much more easily
quiz.why: Wet skin lets electricity through far more easily than dry skin, so a shock is more likely. Picking 'rusty' is a real problem for switches over time, but it is not the danger to you.

quiz.p: How many volts is a wall socket in India?
quiz.why: Mains electricity in India is 230 volts, about 150 times as much as an AA cell's 1.5 volts. That is why sockets are never for experiments.

quiz.p: Kiran, a girl in Class 3, stands a bulb on top of an AA cell. It does not light. What does she need to add?
opts: A wire from the bulb's metal side to the bottom of the cell
quiz.why: The bulb's tip touches only the top of the cell. The electricity needs a path back to the bottom of the cell, through the bulb's side. One wire makes the loop complete. Pressing harder does not make a path.

quiz.p: In a working circuit, you lift a wire off the bulb, on the side away from the cell. What happens?
opts: The bulb goes out at once
quiz.why: A gap anywhere in the loop stops the flow everywhere at once. Picking 'stays lit' means thinking electricity flows into the bulb and stops. It actually goes round and back to the cell.

quiz.p: Which of these is a conductor?
quiz.why: Steel is a metal, and metals are conductors, so the spoon lights the bulb in a circuit tester. Wood, plastic and glass are insulators.

quiz.p: Meenakshi tests a paper clip with a pink plastic coat. The bulb does not light. Why?
opts: The plastic coat is an insulator, so the electricity cannot reach the steel
quiz.why: The steel inside conducts, but the wire ends touch only plastic. Scrape the plastic off each end, and the bulb lights. Colour has nothing to do with it.

quiz.p: Why are electric wires made of copper covered in plastic?
opts: Copper conducts and plastic insulates, so electricity flows inside and stays away from us
Both are conductors, to make it faster
quiz.why: Copper is a metal and a very good conductor, so it carries the electricity. Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps the electricity inside the wire and away from our hands.

quiz.p: A switch is turned off. What is inside it?
opts: A gap of air between two metal parts
quiz.why: When a switch is off, its metal parts are apart, with air between them. Air is an insulator, so the loop is broken. When it is on, they touch and the loop is complete.

quiz.p: Why was the paper clip switch built on cardboard and not on a steel plate?
opts: Steel would join the pins, so the bulb would never turn off
Steel would make the bulb dimmer
quiz.why: Steel is a conductor. It would join the two pins all the time, so opening the clip would not break the loop. Cardboard is an insulator, so only the clip can join the pins.

quiz.p: When a bulb lights, what happens to the electrons in the wire?
opts: They are used up in the bulb
They go round the loop and come back to the cell
They stay still and the bulb pulls in light
quiz.why: The electrons go round the loop and come back. The same ones go round again and again. What the cell uses up is the energy in its chemicals. Picking 'used up' is the common idea that a cell is a tank of electricity.

quiz.p: Galvani thought the twitching frog legs were caused by electricity inside the frog. What did Volta show?
opts: Frogs make no electricity at all
Two different metals with something wet between them make electricity, even with no frog
The twitching was caused by the weather
quiz.why: Volta made electricity with discs of two metals and salty cloth, with no frog, and built the first battery in 1799. Galvani was partly right too, because nerves really do use electrical signals. Picking 'frogs make no electricity' goes too far.

items.p: Sort these things you might find at home. Does each one run on mains electricity from the wall, or on cells?
items.a: see items
items.why: Things with a wire and a plug use mains electricity. Things with a little door for cells run on cells. A strong sorter looks for the plug or the cell door, not for how big the thing is.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, says, "A ceiling fan and a torch both use electricity, so they get it the same way." How can you tell, just by looking, that they do not?
items.a: The fan has a wire going into the wall, so it uses mains electricity. The torch has no wire. It has cells inside, behind a little cap or door. So they get their electricity in different ways.
items.why: A strong answer names what you can see: a wire and a plug for mains, a cell door for cells.

items.p: Grown-ups tell children never to plug in or pull out plugs. Give the reason behind this rule, not just the rule.
items.a: A wall socket in India is 230 volts. That is a strong enough push to send electricity through a person's body and badly hurt or kill them. Fingers can slip onto the metal pins while a plug is going in or coming out, so grown-ups do it.
items.why: A strong answer gives the number, 230 volts, and says what can go wrong: fingers touching the metal pins.

items.p: Divya joins a wire from the top of a cell to the tip of a bulb. She joins a second wire from the bottom of the cell to the tip of the bulb too. The bulb stays dark. What went wrong?
opts: Both wires touch the same place on the bulb, so the electricity does not go through the bulb
items.why: A bulb has two metal contacts: the tip at the bottom and the metal side. The electricity must go in at one and out at the other, through the thin wire inside the bulb. With both wires on the tip, it never passes through the bulb.

items.p: Draw a cell, a bulb and two wires joined so that the bulb lights. Then draw arrows to show the path of the electricity, all the way round.
items.a: A loop: from one end of the cell, along a wire to the bulb's tip, through the bulb, out of its metal side, along the second wire, and back to the other end of the cell. The arrows go round in one direction.
items.why: A strong drawing has no gaps, uses both contacts of the bulb, and brings the path back to the other end of the cell.
items.art: A blank box with a small cell drawn at the bottom and a small bulb drawn at the top.

items.p: You test each of these in a circuit tester. Sort them. Will the bulb light, or stay dark?
items.a: see items
items.why: The metal things are conductors, so they complete the loop. Plastic, rubber, wood and paper are insulators, so they leave a gap.

items.p: In the conductor test, what did all the things that lit the bulb have in common?
items.why: Every thing that lit the bulb was metal. Shiny is not the reason: a glass bangle is shiny but does not conduct. Hard is not the reason either: wood is hard, and soft foil conducts.

items.p: Aluminium foil is thin and soft, not hard like a key. So foil will not light the bulb.
items.why: False. Foil is a metal, so it is a conductor, however thin and soft it is. What matters is the material, not how hard or thick it is.

items.p: A material that lets electricity through, like copper or steel, is called a ____.
items.why: Conductors let electricity flow through them. Most conductors are metals.

items.p: A switch works by making or closing a ____ in the circuit.
items.why: When a switch is off, there is a gap and the loop is broken. When it is on, the gap closes and the loop is complete.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: a material that lets electricity through
opens and closes a gap in a circuit
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These five words come up all through the unit. Knowing them makes the rest easier to explain.

items.p: Shalini's lamp wire has a crack in the plastic, and shiny copper shows through. Why is this dangerous? What should she do?
items.a: The copper is a conductor and carries electricity from the wall, at 230 volts. The plastic was the insulator that kept it away from hands. Now a finger could touch the copper and get a shock. She should not touch it, and should tell a grown-up, who switches off and unplugs the lamp.
items.why: A strong answer says what the copper does, what the plastic was doing, and what to do: don't touch, tell a grown-up.

items.p: A bulb in a circuit is lit. Where does the electricity go after it has passed through the bulb?
opts: It stays inside the bulb and is used up
It carries on along the wire, back to the cell
It leaks out into the air as light
items.why: The electricity goes on round the loop, back to the cell. That is why a wire is needed on both sides of the bulb. The light comes from energy the cell gives, not from the electricity leaking away.

items.p: A torch bulb lights whichever way round you join it to the cell.
items.why: True. A torch bulb lights either way round, because the electricity just needs a complete loop through it. A small LED light is different: it lights only one way round.

items.p: A doorbell rings only while you press the button. What happens inside the button when you press it, and when you let go?
items.a: When I press, two metal parts inside touch, so the loop is complete and the bell rings. When I let go, a spring pushes them apart. Now there is a gap of air, the loop is broken, and the bell stops.
items.why: A strong answer uses the idea of a gap: touching metal closes the loop, a gap of air breaks it.

items.p: Arjun makes a loop with a wire 2 metres long, as long as a door is tall. She closes the gap. When does the bulb light?
items.why: The bulb lights at once. The tiny moving bits called electrons are already in the wire all the way round. The cell pushes them all at the same moment, so none has to travel from the cell to the bulb first.

items.p: When you push a cycle pedal, the back wheel turns at once, even though each link of the chain moves slowly. How is a circuit like a cycle chain?
items.a: In a circuit, the wire is full of electrons all the way round, like the chain is full of links. The cell pushes them all at once, like the pedal pushes the whole chain. So the bulb lights at once, even though each electron moves very slowly.
items.why: A strong answer matches the parts: links and electrons, pedal and cell, wheel and bulb. It says why the bulb lights at once.

items.p: When a cell goes flat, it has run out of electrons.
items.why: False. The electrons go round the loop and come back to the cell. What a flat cell has used up is the energy stored in its chemicals. Many people think a cell is a tank of electricity, but it is more like a pump.

items.p: In the two-cell test, you join two cells in a row, both facing the same way, with one bulb. What does the bulb do?
opts: It is brighter than with one cell
It is dimmer than with one cell
It is the same as with one cell
items.why: Two cells in a row, facing the same way, push together. That is 3 volts instead of 1.5 volts, so more electricity flows and the bulb is brighter.

items.p: Ishita puts two cells into a torch. One goes in bump first, the other flat end first. The torch stays dark. What is really wrong?
opts: The two cells push against each other, so their pushes cancel
One of the cells must be flat
items.why: Each cell pushes one way round the loop. Turned round, the second cell pushes back just as hard, so there is no push at all. Turning it round fixes it. Before blaming the torch, check which way the cells face.

items.p: A wire joined straight from one end of a cell to the other, with nothing else in the loop, is called a ____ circuit.
items.why: A short circuit has no bulb in it. The bulb was what slowed the flow, so now a lot flows, the wire gets hot and the cell runs down fast.

items.p: Why does the wire in a short circuit get hot, when the wires in a circuit with a bulb stay cool?
items.a: The thin wire inside a bulb slows the flow of electricity. Without the bulb, nothing slows it, so a lot of electricity rushes round. All that flow heats the wire. With a bulb in the loop, less flows, so the wires stay cool and the bulb's thin wire glows instead.
items.why: A strong answer says the bulb slows the flow, and more flow means more heat.

items.p: Pencil lead is made of a material called graphite. Touched to both ends of the tester, it makes the bulb glow very dimly. What does that show?
opts: Graphite conducts, but much less well than metal
items.why: A dim glow means some electricity got through, but less than through a metal. So graphite is a conductor that is not a metal. Not every conductor is a metal, though most are.

items.p: Each of these is touched to both ends of a circuit tester. Sort them. Will the bulb light, or stay dark?
items: paper clip with a plastic coat
the same clip with the coat scraped off the ends
a pencil, touching only the wood
items.a: see items
items.why: Only the material the wire ends touch matters. A plastic coat, wood or tape is an insulator and leaves a gap, even with metal inside. Pencil lead lights the bulb only dimly.

items.p: An old string of festival lights goes dark when just one bulb breaks. Why?
opts: The broken bulb makes a gap in the one loop that all the bulbs share
All the other bulbs broke at the same moment
The plug got too hot and switched off
items.why: In old light strings, every bulb is in one loop. A broken bulb leaves a gap, so electricity stops flowing through all of them. Many new strings are wired so that each bulb has its own path.

items.p: Put these in order, from the weakest push to the strongest.
items: two AA cells in a row
a: two AA cells in a row
items.why: One AA cell is 1.5 volts. Two in a row facing the same way are 3 volts. A wall socket is 230 volts, about 150 times one cell, which is why it is never for experiments.

items.p: Draw a circuit with a cell, a bulb and a paper clip switch. Draw it twice: once with the switch open, once with it closed.
items.a: Two loops. In the open one, the clip is off one pin, there is a gap, and the bulb is dark. In the closed one, the clip touches both pins and the bulb is lit.
items.why: The only difference between the two drawings is the gap at the switch. A strong drawing shows that clearly.

items.p: Your torch does not light. Write three things you would check, and say why you would check each one.
items.a: I would check that both cells face the same way, because cells facing opposite ways cancel. I would check the spring and the metal contacts for crust or rust, because those make a gap. I would try new cells, because the old ones may be flat.
items.why: A strong answer hunts for gaps in the loop and thinks about the cells, with a reason for each check.

items.p: A family is deciding who should change the cells in the torch and the TV remote.

views.says: Children can do it. A 1.5 volt cell cannot hurt dry hands, and they learn how a circuit works.
Children should not handle cells at all. Small button cells can be swallowed by the baby.
I can change big AA cells myself, but button cells should stay with a grown-up.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with a fact: an AA cell is only 1.5 volts, so it is safe to touch, but a swallowed button cell can badly burn a child's food pipe within two hours. It then admits a fair point from another side.
items.why: There is a real trade-off here. Children learn by doing, and AA cells are safe to touch. But button cells are dangerous for babies, so where they are kept matters.

items.p: In an old torch, the spring is covered in a white crust from a cell that leaked. New cells face the right way. The torch stays dark. Why?
opts: The crust does not let electricity through, so it makes a gap at the spring
The crust makes the cells weaker
items.why: The crust is not shiny metal, and it is a poor conductor. It sits between the spring and the cell, so the loop has a gap. Scrubbing the spring clean closes the gap.

items.p: Tap water lets a little electricity through, because of the salts dissolved in it.
items.why: True. Very pure water hardly conducts, but tap water has salts dissolved in it. That is one reason water near sockets and switches is dangerous.

items.p: In the 1790s, two Italian scientists argued about why a dead frog's leg twitched when touched with two different metals.

views.says: The electricity comes from the frog. Living bodies have their own electricity, and the metals only let it flow.
The electricity comes from the two different metals touching something wet. The frog's leg only shows that electricity is there.

items.ask: Which scientist do you side with? Give your evidence. Then say what the other scientist got right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence. For Volta: his pile of zinc, copper and salty cloth made electricity with no frog at all. For Galvani: our nerves and muscles really do use electrical signals. A strong answer then gives the other side its due, because both were partly right.
items.why: Volta was right that two metals and something wet make electricity, and he built the first battery in 1799. Galvani was right that living bodies use electricity. Each was partly right.

items.p: Galvani's test had a brass hook, an iron rail and a wet frog's leg. Volta's pile had zinc discs, copper discs and cloth soaked in salty water. What did both set-ups have in common?
items.a: Both had two different metals: brass and iron, or zinc and copper. Both had something wet and salty between them: the frog's leg or the salty cloth. Two different metals with something wet between them make electricity.
items.why: A strong answer finds both things they share: two different metals, and something wet between them.

items.p: Galvani was completely wrong about animal electricity.
items.why: False. Galvani was wrong that the electricity in his test came from the frog. But he was right that living bodies use electricity. Your nerves carry electrical signals to your muscles.

items.p: A touch-me-not plant folds their leaves when you touch them. What travels along the leaf stalk to make this happen?
items.why: A touch starts an electrical signal that travels along the leaf stalk, and the leaves fold. Jagadish Chandra Bose measured electrical signals in plants in Kolkata over a hundred years ago.

items.p: A crow sits on a power line and is not hurt. A person standing on the ground who touches the same line can be killed. Why the difference?
opts: The crow touches only one wire, so there is no loop through their body
Crows have thick feathers that are conductors
The person is heavier than the crow
items.why: Electricity flows only round a loop. The crow touches one wire and nothing else, so there is no path through their body. The person also touches the ground, so there is a path through the body to the earth.

items.p: Why does a plug have at least two pins?
opts: The electricity needs a way in and a way back, to make a loop
So that the plug stands up straight
items.why: An iron or a fan is part of a loop, just like a bulb. The electricity needs one path in and one path back. Many plugs have a third pin, called earth, for safety.

items.p: Put these in order, following the electricity from the socket, round an iron and back.
items: the heating coil inside the iron
the other wire in the cable
the other pin, back into the socket
a: the heating coil inside the iron
the other wire in the cable
the other pin, back into the socket
items.why: An iron is one big loop, like a torch. The electricity goes out through one pin and wire, through the coil that gets hot, and back through the other wire and pin.

items.p: Your friend says, "A cell is like a water tank full of electricity, and the bulb drinks it up." What would you tell her? Use evidence from your experiments.
items.a: I would tell her the electricity is not drunk up. It goes round the loop and back to the cell. My evidence is that a gap after the bulb puts it out, just like a gap before it. What a cell runs out of is the energy in its chemicals.
items.why: A strong answer corrects the idea and backs it with a result from the gap test.

items.p: Before testing anything, Swati touches the two loose wire ends of her circuit tester together, and the bulb lights. Why is this a good first step?
opts: It shows the tester works, so a dark bulb later means the thing is an insulator, not that the tester is broken
It warms up the bulb so it lights faster
items.why: A dark bulb could mean two things: the thing is an insulator, or the tester itself has a gap or a flat cell. Checking that the tester lights on its own rules out the second. A good scientist checks the tool before trusting a result.

items.p: In a steady hand game, the bulb lights when the wand touches the foil path. Sunitha covers the start of the path with tape, so she can rest the wand there. Why does this work?
opts: Tape is an insulator, so touching it leaves a gap
items.why: The wand and the path are the two sides of a gap. Touching metal to metal closes it. Tape is an insulator, so the gap stays open and the bulb stays dark.

items.p: Design a steady hand game. Draw the foil path, the wand, the cell and the bulb, and mark where the gap is.
items.a: A wavy foil path joined to one end of the cell. A wand joined to the bulb, and the bulb joined to the other end of the cell. The gap is between the wand and the path.
items.why: The game works because the wand and the path are the two ends of a gap. A shaky hand closes it.

items.p: Draw a loop with one cell, one bulb and two paper clip switches, so the bulb lights only when both switches are closed.
items.a: One loop with both switches in it, one after the other. If either switch is open, there is a gap, so the bulb is dark. Only when both are closed is the loop complete.
items.why: A strong drawing puts both switches in the same loop, so each one can make a gap. A machine that must not start by accident can use two switches like this.

items.p: An electrician's gloves are made of thick rubber. Why rubber, and not cotton?
opts: Rubber is an insulator, and it stays one even when it is wet
Cotton is too hot to wear
items.why: Rubber stops electricity, and water cannot soak into it. Cotton soaks up sweat and water, and wet cloth lets electricity through. So rubber keeps the hands safe.

items.p: Three AA cells sit in a row. Two face the same way, and the third is turned round. Together they push with ____ volts.
items.why: The two cells facing the same way push with 3 volts. The turned-round cell pushes back with 1.5 volts. 3 minus 1.5 leaves 1.5 volts, the same as one cell on its own.

items.p: Your nerves carry electrical signals, and so does a touch-me-not plant. Is a thought just electricity? Write what you think, and why.
items.a: Any honest answer with a reason. For example: signals in the brain are electrical, and scientists can measure them. But nobody can measure what a thought feels like from the inside. So I think a thought is more than the signals.
items.why: This is an open question that scientists and thinkers still argue about. A strong answer gives a view and a reason.

applications: Every light, fan and appliance at home is part of a circuit with a switch.
Torches, remotes, clocks and toys run on cells in a small circuit.
Electricians use insulated tools and rubber gloves, because plastic and rubber are insulators.
Thick aluminium wires on tall towers carry electricity from power stations to towns. Copper wires carry it inside our homes.
A fridge light uses a press switch that closes when the door opens.
Circuit breakers, called MCBs, in your home's switch box open the circuit by themselves if too much electricity flows.
Phones, computers and cars are full of tiny circuits.
Doctors record the heart's electrical signals with an ECG machine.
Solar panels on roofs make electricity from sunlight and send it round circuits.

open_questions.q: How exactly does the brain turn electrical signals into thoughts and feelings?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists can record the signals, but nobody knows how they become the experience of seeing, feeling or thinking.

open_questions.q: Can we make wires that carry electricity with no loss at all, at room temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Some materials, called superconductors, do this when very cold. Nobody has yet found one that works at room temperature and normal air pressure.

open_questions.q: How can we store enough electricity from sunlight and wind for the night, cheaply?
open_questions.why_open: Batteries are getting better every year, but storing electricity for a whole city is still costly. Scientists are testing many kinds.

open_questions.q: What did the 'Baghdad battery', an ancient clay jar with copper and iron inside, really do?
open_questions.why_open: Some people think it was a battery. Most archaeologists think it was a jar for storing scrolls. Nobody knows for sure.

maths.problem: A wall socket in India pushes at 230 volts. An AA cell pushes at 1.5 volts. Two AA cells in a row push at 3 volts. How many AA cells in a row would push as hard as 30 volts?
maths.explain: Each cell adds 1.5 volts. Two cells make 3 volts. 30 is 10 lots of 3. So 10 lots of 2 cells, which is 20 cells. Check: 20 times 1.5 is 30.
maths.context: This is about cells in a row. Each AA cell adds 1.5 volts of push.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups shows how fast the push adds up, and how far a cell is from a wall socket.

maths.problem: In the Conductor Test, Arjun tested 12 things. 5 lit the bulb brightly, 1 lit it very dimly, and the rest did not light it. How many did not light it? What fraction of the things lit the bulb at all?
maths.answer: 6 did not light it. Half of the things lit the bulb at all.
maths.explain: 5 + 1 = 6 lit the bulb. 12 - 6 = 6 did not. 6 out of 12 is the same as 1 out of 2, which is a half.
maths.context: This is about the Conductor Test, where you touch the two wire ends of a tester to different things and see if the bulb lights.
maths.why_maths: A fraction says what share of the things conducted, so you can compare it with a friend who tested a different number of things.

maths.problem: A wall clock uses one AA cell for about 12 months. A TV remote uses two AA cells, and they last about 6 months. How many cells does each use in 2 years?
maths.answer: The clock uses 2 cells. The remote uses 8 cells.
maths.explain: The clock needs 1 cell every 12 months. 2 years is 24 months, so 2 cells. The remote needs 2 cells every 6 months. 24 months is 4 lots of 6, so 4 times 2 is 8 cells.
maths.context: This is about how long cells last in things at home. The numbers are typical, and yours may be different.
maths.why_maths: Working out how many cells a family uses helps you see why spent cells need to be collected and recycled, not thrown away.

maths.problem: Kavya builds a loop with 4 wires, a bulb and a cell. She can make a gap at any one join. The loop has 6 joins. If she makes a gap at a different join each time, how many times will the bulb go out?
maths.explain: A gap anywhere in the loop stops the bulb. There are 6 joins, so all 6 gaps stop it. This is a reasoning problem: the answer comes from knowing the rule, not from counting.
maths.context: This is about the Where Is the Gap? experiment, where you break a loop in different places.
maths.why_maths: Reasoning from a rule lets you predict every result without testing each one.

maths.problem: Each electron in a wire moves about 1 millimetre in 10 seconds. How long would one electron take to travel round a loop of wire 1 metre long? A metre is 1000 millimetres.
maths.answer: About 10,000 seconds, which is nearly 3 hours.
maths.explain: 1000 millimetres, at 1 millimetre every 10 seconds, takes 1000 times 10 = 10,000 seconds. An hour is 3600 seconds, so that is nearly 3 hours. Yet the bulb lights at once, because all the electrons start moving together.
maths.context: This is about how slowly each electron moves in a wire, compared with how quickly a bulb lights.
maths.why_maths: The big number shows that the bulb cannot be waiting for electrons to arrive from the cell. They were already in the wire.

roots.context: We have built circuits, broken them, and found what lets electricity through. Now we ask what a circuit tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your bulb lit only when a second path led back to the cell. So the electricity does not stop in the bulb. It goes round and comes back to the cell. The bulb is not using up electrons, only the energy the cell gives them as they pass.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a cell as a tank full of electricity that the bulb drinks up. But the electrons that flow are part of the wire itself, and they come back. What a cell runs out of is the energy in its chemicals, not electrons.
deep_truth.evidence: In the bulb challenge, the bulb stayed dark with one wire from the cell to its tip. It lit only when a path also led back to the other end of the cell. In Where Is the Gap?, a gap after the bulb put it out too.

three.who_am_i: Every move you make starts with electrical signals running along your nerves to your muscles.
three.what_is_life: A touch-me-not feels a touch and sends an electrical signal along their leaf stalk, and their leaves fold.
three.what_is_this_world: Lightning, a torch and the fan above you all work because charges move.

roots.thread: In a wire with no cell, the electrons drift about in every direction. Their movements add up to nothing. Join a cell, and one steady push sets them all moving round the loop together. That one flow can light a bulb, spin a fan, ring a bell or warm an iron. Many different jobs come from one simple movement of charges that were there all along.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes share one hub. It is the empty space at the centre that makes the wheel useful. We shape clay into a pot, and it is the empty inside that holds what we want.
teachings.link: A switch is useful because of its gap. The air gap is what lets us turn a light off. A circuit works through its metal, but we control it through its empty space.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu to put salt in water overnight. In the morning the boy cannot see the salt. But he tastes the water from the top, the middle and the bottom, and it is salty everywhere.
teachings.link: The electrons were in every part of the wire before you joined the cell, though you could not see them. The bulb lighting at once is how you could tell, the way the taste told Shvetaketu the salt was there.

science.text: Electric charge is never made or destroyed. A cell moves charges round a circuit, using energy from its chemicals.
Nerves, the heart and many plants send signals by moving charged particles in and out of their cells.
How the brain's electrical signals become thoughts and feelings is not known.

other_view.view: A circuit is electrons pushed round by a chemical reaction, and nothing more. Comparing it with a wheel's empty hub or with hidden salt is a nice picture. But it tells us nothing new about the wire.

practice.title: The family circuit
practice.say: Let's stand in a circle and hold hands. Close your eyes. I will squeeze the hand on my right. When you feel a squeeze, pass it on to the next person. Let's see it come back to me. Now one person lets go. I squeeze again. Does it come back? Hold hands again and breathe slowly three times.
practice.kid: Hold hands in a circle. Close your eyes. Feel a squeeze? Pass it on. Did it come back? Now someone lets go. Does it still come back?

ask: The electrons in your circuit were already in the wire. So what did joining the cell really change?
A switch works because of a gap. Can an empty space do a job?
Your thoughts travel as electrical signals. Is a thought something that moves, or something more?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. Choices made: only AA cells are used, never sockets or chargers. Torch bulbs are used, not LEDs, because an LED will not light from one 1.5 volt cell and lights only one way round. A 2.5 volt bulb glows only dimly on one cell, so the steps say to dim the room, and the two-cell experiment shows it brighter. No cell holder? The wires can be taped to the cell's ends. Foil folded four times lengthwise works as wire, but a foil strip held across both ends of a cell gets warm, so every step warns against short circuits. The pencil test may give only a very faint glow, or none, with a bulb, so the step says so and suggests a short piece of lead. Plastic-coated paper clips are a deliberate surprise in the Conductor Test. Tap and salty water tests were left out, because a bulb on one or two AA cells does not visibly glow through water. The torch activity skips torches with built-in rechargeable batteries. Leaked cells leave a crust that should be wiped with a dry cloth, followed by hand washing. Button cells are named as dangerous for babies. Both games work for one child alone. The spine is the bulb challenge, the safety walk, the Conductor Test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani, a doctor in Bologna in Italy, was studying how frog legs move. His wife, Lucia Galeazzi, also worked in his laboratory. Galvani found that a dead frog's leg twitched when he touched it with two different metals, such as a brass hook and an iron rail. In 1791 he wrote that the frog had their own 'animal electricity' in their body, and the metals let it flow. Alessandro Volta, a physicist in Pavia, repeated the experiments. He thought the electricity came from the two metals, and the frog only showed it. To prove it, he left the frog out. He piled up discs of zinc and copper, with card soaked in salty water between them. The pile gave a steady flow of electricity, and he could feel it as a tingle. In 1800 he described it in a letter to the Royal Society in London. It was the first battery. So Galvani's idea that the metals' electricity came from the frog was wrong. But he was right that living bodies use electricity. Our nerves really do send electrical signals.
how_we_found_out.who: Luigi Galvani, a doctor in Bologna, and Alessandro Volta, a physicist in Pavia
how_we_found_out.when: 1791 (Galvani's book on animal electricity) and 1799 to 1800 (Volta's pile)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Galvani thought the electricity that made the frog legs twitch was stored in the frog's body. Volta showed that two different metals with something salty and wet between them make electricity on their own, with no frog. Galvani was still right that nerves use electricity.
